theme: Genetics, DNA & The Tree of Evolution
title: Genetics, DNA & The Tree of Evolution
description: A 60-question grand master assessment exploring DNA double-helix architecture, protein synthesis, Mendelian inheritance, natural selection, CRISPR, and deep time genomics.

questions.question: What three chemical components compose a single monomeric nucleotide unit of DNA?
options: Deoxyribose sugar, phosphate group, nitrogenous base
Ribose sugar, fatty acid, amine group
questions.explanation: A nucleotide consists of a 5-carbon deoxyribose sugar ring bonded to a phosphate group at the 5-prime carbon and a nitrogenous base at the 1-prime carbon.

questions.question: In double-stranded DNA, what nitrogenous pyrimidine base always pairs with the purine adenine via two hydrogen bonds?
questions.explanation: According to Chargaff rules, adenine pairs exclusively with thymine (A=T via two hydrogen bonds), while guanine pairs with cytosine (G=C via three bonds).

questions.question: Who produced Photo 51 in 1952, the iconic X-ray diffraction image that revealed the B-form double-helical structure of DNA?
questions.explanation: Working at King College London with Raymond Gosling, Rosalind Franklin captured the high-resolution X-ray diffraction photograph confirming the DNA helical lattice.

questions.question: What covalent chemical bond links adjacent nucleotides together along the continuous sugar-phosphate backbone of a nucleic acid strand?
questions.explanation: A phosphodiester bond connects the 3-prime hydroxyl group of one deoxyribose sugar to the 5-prime phosphate group of the neighboring nucleotide.

questions.question: In single-stranded RNA molecules, what nitrogenous base replaces thymine to pair complementarily with adenine?
questions.explanation: RNA uses uracil instead of thymine; uracil lacks the methyl group present on carbon-5 of thymine and requires less cellular energy to produce.

questions.question: How many hydrogen bonds form specifically between a guanine and cytosine G-C base pair in double-stranded DNA?
questions.explanation: G-C base pairs share three hydrogen bonds compared to two in A-T pairs, making DNA regions with high G-C content thermally more stable.

questions.question: What primary enzyme transcribes a complementary messenger RNA strand from a DNA template strand during gene transcription?
questions.explanation: RNA Polymerase unwinds the double helix and synthesizes an RNA transcript in the 5-prime to 3-prime direction using ribose nucleotides.

questions.question: What three-nucleotide sequence on a messenger RNA molecule specifies a single amino acid or translation stop signal?
questions.explanation: Each mRNA triplet codon corresponds to a specific amino acid delivered by a transfer RNA molecule bearing the complementary anticodon.

questions.question: What cellular ribonucleoprotein complex translates mRNA codons into a growing polypeptide chain of amino acids?
questions.explanation: Ribosomes consist of large and small subunits composed of ribosomal RNA and proteins that catalyze peptide bond formation at aminoacyl and peptidyl sites.

questions.question: What non-coding nucleotide segments are spliced out of eukaryotic pre-mRNA transcripts by spliceosomes before translation?
questions.explanation: Introns are intervening non-coding regions removed during RNA splicing, allowing alternative splicing of exons to generate multiple protein variants from one gene.

questions.question: What universal start codon in messenger RNA signals the beginning of translation and codes for the amino acid methionine?
questions.explanation: AUG is the universal start codon in all domains of life, recognized by initiator tRNA charged with methionine (or formylmethionine in bacteria).

questions.question: How many possible distinct triplet codons exist in the standard universal genetic code table composed of four RNA bases?
questions.explanation: Four nucleotides arranged in groups of three yield 64 possible codons (4x4x4): 61 codons specifying 20 amino acids and 3 termination stop codons.

questions.question: Who is celebrated as the father of genetics for discovering foundational laws of inheritance through breeding experiments on garden pea plants?
questions.explanation: Mendel, an Augustinian friar in Brno, tracked seven discrete traits in Pisum sativum, publishing his laws of inheritance in 1866.

questions.question: What Mendelian principle states that two alleles for a heritable trait segregate during gamete formation so each gamete carries only one allele?
questions.explanation: Mendel First Law states that homologous chromosome separation during meiosis ensures haploid gametes receive only a single copy of each gene.

questions.question: What genetic grid diagram is used to predict the phenotypic and genotypic probability ratios of offspring resulting from parental crosses?
questions.explanation: Devised by British geneticist Reginald Punnett in 1905, the square visualizes all possible combinations of maternal and paternal alleles.

questions.question: What non-Mendelian inheritance pattern occurs when both alleles in a heterozygous individual are simultaneously and fully expressed in the phenotype?
questions.explanation: In human AB blood type, both A and B glycosyltransferase enzymes are expressed equally, producing both A and B antigens on red blood cell surfaces.

questions.question: What term describes a genetic phenomenon where a single gene locus influences multiple distinct, seemingly unrelated phenotypic traits?
questions.explanation: Sickle cell anemia is a classic pleiotropic mutation: a single point mutation in beta-globin causes anemia, organ damage, and malaria resistance.

questions.question: In a classic Mendelian monohybrid cross between two heterozygous parents (Bb x Bb), what percentage of offspring exhibit the dominant phenotype?
questions.explanation: The monohybrid cross yields a genotypic ratio of 1 BB : 2 Bb : 1 bb, resulting in 75 percent dominant phenotype and 25 percent recessive phenotype.

questions.question: How many homologous pairs of chromosomes are present in somatic cell nuclei of a typical human?
questions.explanation: Humans possess 22 pairs of autosomes and one pair of sex chromosomes (XX in females, XY in males), totaling 46 chromosomes per diploid cell.

questions.question: What repetitive non-coding DNA caps on chromosome ends protect genetic data from degradation, shortening with each somatic cell division?
questions.explanation: Human telomeres consist of tandem TTAGGG hexanucleotide repeats protected by shelterin protein complexes that prevent end-to-end chromosome fusion.

questions.question: During what stage of meiosis do non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes exchange genetic segments via crossing over at chiasmata?
questions.explanation: Synaptonemal complexes align homologous pairs during Prophase I, facilitating homologous recombination that generates novel allele combinations.

questions.question: What constricted chromosomal region holds sister chromatids together and serves as the assembly site for spindle microtubule kinetochores?
questions.explanation: Centromeres contain specialized CENP-A histone variants that anchor the kinetochore protein complex to pull chromatids apart during anaphase.

questions.question: What human chromosomal condition is caused by non-disjunction producing trisomy of chromosome 21?
questions.explanation: Trisomy 21 results from the presence of three copies of chromosome 21 instead of two, causing developmental differences and characteristic facial features.

questions.question: How many total chromosomes are contained inside a normal human diploid somatic cell nucleus?
questions.explanation: Human somatic cells contain exactly 46 chromosomes (2n = 46), with 23 inherited from each parent via haploid gametes.

questions.question: Who independently conceived the theory of evolution by natural selection in the Malay Archipelago, prompting joint publication with Charles Darwin in 1858?
questions.explanation: Wallace sent his essay on natural selection to Darwin from Indonesia in 1858, leading to joint presentation at the Linnean Society of London.

questions.question: What evolutionary mechanism causes random, non-adaptive fluctuations in allele frequencies within small populations due to chance sampling events?
questions.explanation: Genetic drift, including founder events and population bottlenecks, can cause neutral or slightly deleterious alleles to become fixed purely by chance.

questions.question: What mode of natural selection simultaneously favors phenotypic extremes at both ends of a distribution curve over intermediate phenotypes?
questions.explanation: Disruptive selection occurs when environmental niches favor two distinct morphs, such as small-billed and large-billed seedcrackers, driving divergence.

questions.question: What phenomenon occurs when a severe catastrophe dramatically reduces population size, eliminating vast amounts of genetic diversity?
questions.explanation: Cheetahs underwent a severe Pleistocene bottleneck roughly 10,000 years ago, resulting in near-identical genetic homogeneity and high graft tolerance today.

questions.question: What rapid evolutionary process occurs when a single ancestral species diversifies into multiple ecologically specialized species filling diverse niches?
questions.explanation: Classic examples of adaptive radiation include Darwin finches on the Galapagos Islands, Hawaiian silverswords, and African Rift Lake cichlids.

questions.question: In what year CE did Charles Darwin publish his landmark scientific treatise On the Origin of Species?
questions.explanation: Charles Darwin published On the Origin of Species on November 24, 1859, laying out comprehensive evidence for common descent and natural selection.

questions.question: What mode of speciation occurs when a physical geographic barrier like a mountain range or ocean separates a population into isolated groups?
questions.explanation: Geographic isolation halts gene flow between populations, allowing genetic drift and local natural selection to accumulate reproductive barriers over time.

questions.question: What anatomical structures share a common evolutionary ancestral skeletal blueprint despite performing completely different functions today?
questions.explanation: The pentadactyl limb framework found in human arms, bat wings, whale flippers, and mole paws illustrates divergent evolution from a common tetrapod ancestor.

questions.question: What term describes reduced, non-functional anatomical remnants of ancestral organs, such as the pelvic bone remnants in baleen whales?
questions.explanation: Vestigial features reflect evolutionary history where structural changes made ancestral organs obsolete, such as flightless cormorant wings or human coccyx bones.

questions.question: What branching diagram illustrates hypothesized evolutionary relationships and shared ancestry among distinct biological clades?
questions.explanation: Phylogenetic trees use molecular sequencing and synapomorphies to map nodes of divergence and trace evolutionary lineage back to common ancestors.

questions.question: What famous transitional fossil discovered on Ellesmere Island in 2004 revealed wrist bones, scales, and neck joints bridging fish and tetrapods?
questions.explanation: Tiktaalik lived 375 million years ago in the Late Devonian, possessing fish gills and scales alongside tetrapod-like wrist joints, ribs, and a mobile neck.

questions.question: How many million years old is the transitional tetrapodomorph fish fossil Tiktaalik roseae from the Late Devonian?
questions.explanation: Tiktaalik fossils discovered in Nunavut, Canada date precisely to 375 million years ago, capturing the transitional evolution of land-walking limbs.

questions.question: Approximately what percentage of DNA sequence identity do modern humans share with chimpanzees Pan troglodytes across alignable bases?
questions.explanation: Whole-genome comparisons between humans and chimpanzees show roughly 98.8 percent nucleotide identity in directly alignable DNA sequences.

questions.question: In what year was the first working draft sequence of the complete Human Genome officially announced by international consortia?
questions.explanation: The International Human Genome Sequencing Consortium and Celera Genomics published concurrent landmark drafts in Nature and Science in February 2001.

questions.question: Approximately what percentage of the 3.2 billion base pairs in the human nuclear genome directly codes for functional protein amino acid sequences?
questions.explanation: Only about 1.5 percent of the human genome consists of protein-coding exons; the remainder consists of introns, regulatory switches, retrotransposons, and structural elements.

questions.question: What non-recombining circular DNA is inherited exclusively through the maternal lineage, allowing geneticists to trace maternal human ancestry?
questions.explanation: Mitochondrial DNA is passed down strictly from mothers in egg cytoplasm, enabling scientists to reconstruct prehistoric maternal human migrations back to Mitochondrial Eve.

questions.question: Approximately what percentage of nuclear DNA in contemporary non-African human populations originates from ancient interbreeding with Neanderthals?
questions.explanation: Genomic sequencing reveals modern Eurasians retain roughly 1 to 2 percent Neanderthal DNA, influencing skin keratins, immune receptors, and metabolic traits.

questions.question: Approximately how many billion base pairs make up a single haploid copy of the human nuclear genome?
questions.explanation: The human haploid genome contains roughly 3.05 to 3.2 billion base pairs distributed across 23 chromosomes.

questions.question: What primary biochemical epigenetic modification adds methyl groups to cytosine bases in CpG islands to silence gene transcription?
questions.explanation: DNA methyltransferases transfer methyl groups to cytosine, blocking transcription factor binding and recruiting repressor proteins to silence genes.

questions.question: What revolutionary targeted gene editing technology adapted from bacterial adaptive immunity uses a guide RNA and nuclease to edit DNA sequences?
questions.explanation: The Cas9 endonuclease binds a synthetic single guide RNA (sgRNA) that directs it to make precise double-strand breaks at complementary genomic targets.

questions.question: What alkaline protein octamers package and wrap nuclear DNA strands into fundamental repeating chromatin beads called nucleosomes?
questions.explanation: DNA wraps roughly 1.65 times around an octamer of core histone proteins (H2A, H2B, H3, H4), with histone tail acetylation loosening chromatin for gene expression.

questions.question: What field of genetics studies heritable changes in gene expression and cellular phenotype that occur without changing the underlying DNA sequence?
questions.explanation: Epigenetics investigates chromatin remodeling, DNA methylation, and non-coding RNA pathways that regulate cell differentiation throughout life.

questions.question: What French biochemist was awarded the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry alongside Jennifer Doudna for the development of CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing?
questions.explanation: Charpentier discovered the essential tracrRNA component in Streptococcus pyogenes before collaborating with Doudna to engineer the programmable two-component CRISPR system.

questions.question: In what year CE was the Nobel Prize in Chemistry awarded to Emmanuelle Charpentier and Jennifer Doudna for CRISPR-Cas9?
questions.explanation: The Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2020 was awarded jointly to Emmanuelle Charpentier and Jennifer A. Doudna for developing a method for genome editing.

questions.question: What evolutionary theory championed by Lynn Margulis explains that eukaryotic mitochondria and chloroplasts originated from engulfed free-living prokaryotes?
questions.explanation: Mitochondria evolved from engulfed aerobic alphaproteobacteria, evidenced by their own circular DNA, double membranes, and bacterial 70S ribosomes.

questions.question: What geological event roughly 541 million years ago saw the rapid evolutionary explosion of nearly all modern animal phyla in the fossil record?
questions.explanation: During the Cambrian period, complex bilateral body plans, mineralized exoskeletons, compound eyes, and predatory niches emerged rapidly over roughly 25 million years.

questions.question: What catastrophic Great Dying mass extinction event 252 million years ago wiped out over 90 percent of marine species and 70 percent of land vertebrates?
questions.explanation: Massive volcanic outpourings from the Siberian Traps released trillions of tons of greenhouse gases, triggering catastrophic ocean anoxia and global warming.

questions.question: What biological milestone 2.4 billion years ago driven by cyanobacterial photosynthesis permanently filled Earth atmosphere with free oxygen gas?
questions.explanation: Cyanobacteria utilizing oxygenic photosynthesis saturated oceanic dissolved iron to deposit banded iron formations before oxygen accumulated in the air.

questions.question: What layered sedimentary rock structures formed by ancient colonies of photosynthetic cyanobacteria provide the oldest fossil records of life on Earth?
questions.explanation: Stromatolite fossils from Western Australia and Greenland date back over 3.5 billion years, formed by cyanobacterial mats trapping and cementing sediment.

questions.question: How many million years ago did the Cambrian Explosion begin, marking the start of the Phanerozoic Eon?
questions.explanation: The Cambrian explosion began approximately 541 million years ago at the base of the Fortunian stage, defining the boundary of the Cambrian period.

questions.question: What molecular biology technique invented by Kary Mullis in 1983 uses thermal cycling to exponentially amplify specific target DNA sequences?
questions.explanation: PCR uses cycles of denaturation (95 °C), primer annealing (55 °C), and extension (72 °C) to generate billions of exact DNA copies within hours.

questions.question: What heat-stable DNA polymerase enzyme isolated from Yellowstone extremophile bacteria Thermus aquaticus makes automated PCR cycling possible?
questions.explanation: Taq polymerase withstands repeated 95 °C denaturation cycles without denaturing, eliminating the need to manually add fresh enzyme after every PCR cycle.

questions.question: In 1996, what mammal became the first cloned animal produced from an adult somatic cell using somatic cell nuclear transfer at the Roslin Institute?
questions.explanation: Ian Wilmut and Keith Campbell transferred the nucleus of an adult Finn-Dorset mammary cell into an enucleated egg cell, proving adult cells remain pluripotency-capable.

questions.question: What analytical technique uses an electric field to separate negatively charged DNA fragments across an agarose gel matrix by molecular length?
questions.explanation: Phosphate backbones give DNA a uniform negative charge; smaller fragments migrate faster toward the positive anode through the porous agarose mesh.

questions.question: What high-throughput DNA sequencing technology sequences millions of DNA fragments simultaneously in parallel, revolutionizing personalized genomics?
questions.explanation: NGS platforms, such as Illumina sequencing-by-synthesis, slashed the cost of sequencing a whole human genome from 100 million dollars to under 300 dollars.

questions.question: In what year CE was Dolly the Sheep born after being cloned from an adult somatic cell at the Roslin Institute in Scotland?
questions.explanation: Dolly the sheep was born on July 5, 1996 at the Roslin Institute, marking a historic breakthrough in mammalian somatic cell cloning.
